But this was the day of his patience and suffering, and he answered him with the <hi type="italic">meekness of wisdom,</hi> to teach us not to avenge ourselves, not to render <hi type="italic">railing for railing,</hi> but with the <hi type="italic">innocency of the dove</hi> to bear injuries, even when with the <hi type="italic">wisdom of the serpent,</hi> as our Saviour, we show the injustice of them, and appeal to the magistrate concerning them. Christ did not here <hi type="italic">turn the other cheek,</hi> by which it appears that that rule, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Matt. v. 39</reference>, is not to be understood literally; a man may possibly <hi type="italic">turn the other cheek,</hi> and yet have his heart full of malice; but, comparing Christ's precept with his pattern, we learn, (1.) That in such cases we must not be our own avengers, nor judges in our own cause. We must rather receive than give the second blow, which makes the quarrel; we are allowed to defend ourselves, but not to avenge ourselves: the magistrate (if it be necessary for the preserving of the public peace, and the restraining and terrifying of evil-doers) is to be the avenger, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>. (2.) Our resentment of injuries done us must always be rational, and never passionate; such Christ's here was; <hi type="italic">when he suffered,</hi> he reasoned, but <hi type="italic">threatened not.</hi> He fairly expostulated with him that did him the injury, and so may we. (3.) When we are called out to suffering, we must <hi type="italic">accommodate ourselves</hi> to the inconveniences of a suffering state, with patience, and by one indignity done us be prepared to receive another, and to make the best of it. <div eID="gen28500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28501" type="x-p"/> VI. While the servants were thus abusing him, Peter was proceeding to deny him, <reference osisRef="John.18.25-John.18.27">v. 25-27</reference>. It is a sad story, and none of the least of Christ's sufferings. <div eID="gen28501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28502" type="x-p"/> 1. He repeated the sin the second time, <reference osisRef="John.18.25">v. 25</reference>. While he was warming himself with the servants, as one of them, they asked him, <hi type="italic">Art not thou one of his disciples?</hi> What dost thou here among us? He, perhaps, hearing that Christ was examined about his disciples, and fearing he should be seized, or at least smitten, as his Master was, if he should own it, flatly denied it, and said, <hi type="italic">I am not.</hi> <div eID="gen28502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28503" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was his great folly to thrust himself into the temptation, by continuing in the company of those that were unsuitable for him, and that he had nothing to do with. He staid to warm himself; but those that warm themselves with evil doers grow cold towards good people and good things, and those that are fond of the devil's fire-side are in danger of the devil's fire. Peter might have stood by his Master at the bar, and have warmed himself better than here, at the fire of his Master's love, which <hi type="italic">many waters could not quench,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.8.6-Song.8.7">Cant. viii. 6, 7</reference>. He might there have warmed himself with zeal for his Master, and indignation at his persecutors; but he chose rather to warm with them than to warm against them. But how could one (one disciple) be warm alone? <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.11">Eccl. iv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen28503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28504" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was his great unhappiness that he was again assaulted by the temptation; and no other could be expected, for this was a place, this an hour, of temptation. When the judge asked Christ about his disciples, probably the servants took the hint, and challenged Peter for one of them, "Answer to thy name." See here, [1.] The subtlety of the tempter in running down one whom he saw falling, and mustering a greater force against him; not a maid now, but all the servants. Note, Yielding to one temptation invites another, and perhaps a stronger. Satan redoubles his attacks when we give ground. [2.] The danger of bad company. We commonly study to approve ourselves to those with whom we choose to associate; we value ourselves upon their good word and covet to stand right in their opinion. As we choose our people we choose our praise, and govern ourselves accordingly; we are therefore concerned to make the first choice well, and not to mingle with those whom we cannot please without displeasing God. <div eID="gen28504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28505" type="x-p"/> (3.) It was his great weakness, nay, it was his great wickedness, to yield to the temptation, and to say, <hi type="italic">I am not one</hi> of his disciples, as one ashamed of that which was his honour, and afraid of suffering for it, which would have been yet more his honour. See how the <hi type="italic">fear of man brings a snare.</hi> When Christ was admired, and caressed, and treated with respect, Peter pleased himself, and perhaps prided himself, in this, that he was a disciple of Christ, and so put in for a share in the honours done to his Master. Thus many who seem fond of the reputation of religion when it is in fashion are ashamed of the reproach of it; but we must take it <hi type="italic">for better and worse.</hi> <div eID="gen28505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28506" type="x-p"/> 2. He repeated the sin the third time, <reference osisRef="John.18.26-John.18.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. Here he was attacked by one of the servants, who was kinsman to Malchus, who, when he heard Peter deny himself to be a disciple of Christ, gave him the lie with great assurance: "<hi type="italic">Did not I see thee in the garden with him?</hi> Witness my kinsman's ear." Peter then denied again, as if he knew nothing of Christ, nothing of the garden, nothing of all this matter. <div eID="gen28506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28507" type="x-p"/> (1.) This third assault of the temptation was more close than the former: before his relation to Christ was only suspected, here it is proved upon him by one that saw him with Jesus, and saw him draw his sword in his defence. Note, Those who by sin think to help themselves out of trouble do but entangle and embarrass themselves the more. Dare to be brave, for truth will out. <hi type="italic">A bird of the air</hi> may perhaps <hi type="italic">tell the matter</hi> which we seek to conceal with a lie. Notice is taken of this servant's being akin to Malchus, because this circumstance would make it the more a terror to Peter. "Now," thinks he, "I am gone, my business is done, there needs no other witness nor prosecutor." We should not make any man in particular our enemy if we can help it, because the time may come when either he or some of his relations may have us at their mercy. He that may need a friend should not make a foe. But observe, though here was sufficient evidence against Peter, and sufficient provocation given by his denial to have prosecuted him, yet he escapes, has no harm done him nor attempted to be done. Note, We are often drawn into sin by groundless causeless fears, which there is no occasion for, and which a small degree of wisdom and resolution would make nothing of. <div eID="gen28507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28508" type="x-p"/> (2.) His yielding to it was no less base than the former: <hi type="italic">He denied again.</hi> See here, [1.] The nature of sin in general: <hi type="italic">the heart is hardened by the deceitfulness of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.13">Heb. iii. 13</reference>. It was a strange degree of effrontery that Peter had arrived to on a sudden, that he could with such assurance stand in a lie against so clear a disproof; but <hi type="italic">the beginning of sin is as the letting forth of water,</hi> when once the fence is broken men easily go from bad to worse. [2.] Of the sin of lying in particular; it is a fruitful sin, and upon this account <hi type="italic">exceedingly sinful:</hi> one lie needs another to support it, and that another. It is a rule in the devil's politics <hi type="italic">Male facta male factis tegere, ne perpluant</hi>—<hi type="italic">To cover sin with sin, in order to escape detection.</hi>
entries.c376848114d14cad07de72ffeeb629d406b26528: <div eID="gen28508" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ in the Judgment-Hall; Christ Arraigned before Pilate.</title> <div sID="gen28509" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Then led they Jesus from Caiaphas unto the hall of judgment: and it was early; and they themselves went not into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled; but that they might eat the passover. <hi type="super">29</hi> Pilate then went out unto them, and said, What accusation bring ye against this man? <hi type="super">30</hi> They answered and said unto him, If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee. <hi type="super">31</hi> Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death: <hi type="super">32</hi> That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spake, signifying what death he should die. 33 Then Pilate entered into the judgment hall again, and called Jesus, and said unto him, Art thou the King of the Jews? 34 Jesus answered him, Sayest thou this thing of thyself, or did others tell it thee of me? <hi type="super">35</hi> Pilate answered, Am I a Jew? Thine own nation and the chief priests have delivered thee unto me: what hast thou done? <hi type="super">36</hi> Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence. <hi type="super">37</hi> Pilate therefore said unto him, Art thou a king then? Jesus answered, Thou sayest that I am a king. To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice. <hi type="super">38</hi> Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault <hi type="italic">at all.</hi> <hi type="super">39</hi> But ye have a custom, that I should release unto you one at the passover: will ye therefore that I release unto you the King of the Jews? <hi type="super">40</hi> Then cried they all again, saying, Not this man, but Barabbas. Now Barabbas was a robber. <div eID="gen28509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28510" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Christ's arraignment before Pilate, the Roman governor, in the <hi type="italic">prætorium</hi> (a Latin word made Greek), the prætor's house, or <hi type="italic">hall of judgment;</hi> thither they hurried him, to get him condemned in the Roman court, and executed by the Roman power. Being resolved on his death, they took this course, 1. That he might be put to death the more legally and regularly, according to the present constitution of their government, since they became a province of the empire; not stoned in a popular tumult, as Stephen, but put to death with the present formalities of justice. Thus he was treated as a malefactor, <hi type="italic">being made sin for us.</hi> 2. That he might be put to death the more safely. If they could engage the Roman government in the matter, which the people stood in awe of, there would be little danger of an uproar. 3. That he might be put to death with more reproach to himself. <hi type="italic">The death of the cross,</hi> which the Romans commonly used, being of all deaths the most ignominious, they were desirous by it to put an indelible mark of infamy upon him, and so to sink his reputation for ever. This therefore they harped upon, <hi type="italic">Crucify him.</hi> 4. That he might be put to death with less reproach to them. It was an invidious thing to put one to death that had done so much good in the world, and therefore they were willing to throw the odium upon the Roman government, to make that the less acceptable to the people, and save themselves from the reproach. Thus many are more afraid of the scandal of a bad action than of the sin of it. See <reference osisRef="Acts.5.28">Acts v. 28</reference>. Two things are here observed concerning the prosecution:—(1.) Their policy and industry in the prosecution: <hi type="italic">It was early;</hi> some think about two or three in the morning, others about five or six, when most people were in their beds; and so there would be the less danger of opposition from the people that were for Christ; while, at the same time, they had their agents about, to call those together whom they could influence to cry out against him. See how much their heart was upon it, and how violent they were in the prosecution. Now that they had him in their hands, they would lose no time till they had him upon the cross, but denied themselves their natural rest, to push on this matter. See <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mic. ii. 1</reference>. (2.) Their superstition and vile hypocrisy: <hi type="italic">The chief priests and elders,</hi> though they came along with the prisoner, that the thing might be done effectually, <hi type="italic">went not into the judgment-hall,</hi> because it was the house of an uncircumcised Gentile, <hi type="italic">lest they should be defiled,</hi> but kept out of doors, <hi type="italic">that they might eat the passover,</hi> not the paschal lamb (that was eaten the night before) but the passover-feast, upon the sacrifices which were offered on the fifteenth day, <hi type="italic">the Chagigah,</hi> as they called it, the passover-bullocks spoken of <reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">Deut. xvi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.24">2 Chron. xxx. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.8-2Chr.35.9">xxxv. 8, 9</reference>. These they were to eat of, and therefore would not go into the court, for fear of touching a Gentile, and thereby contracting, not a legal, but only a traditional pollution. This they scrupled, but made no scruple of breaking through all the laws of equity to persecute Christ to the death. <hi type="italic">They strained at a gnat, and swallowed a camel.</hi> Let us now see what passed at <hi type="italic">the judgment-hall.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen28510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28511" type="x-p"/> I. Pilate's conference with the prosecutors. They were called first, and stated what they had to say against the prisoner, as was very fit, <reference osisRef="John.18.29-John.18.32">v. 29-32</reference>. <div eID="gen28511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28512" type="x-p"/> 1. The judge calls for the indictment. Because they would not come into the hall, <hi type="italic">he went out to them</hi> into the court before the house, to talk with them. Looking upon Pilate as a magistrate, that we may give every one his due, here are three things commendable in him:—(1.) His diligent and close application to business. If it had been upon a good occasion, it had been very well that he was willing to be called up early to the judgment-seat. Men in public trusts must not love their ease. (2.) His condescending to the humour of the people, and receding from the honour of his place to gratify their scruples. He might have said, "If they be so nice as not to come in to me, let them go home as they came;" by the same rule as we might say, "If the complainant scruple to take off his hat to the magistrate, let not his complaint be heard;" but Pilate insists not upon it, bears with them, and goes out to them; for, when it is for good, we should <hi type="italic">become all things to all men.</hi> (3.) His adherence to the rule of justice, in demanding the accusation, suspecting the prosecution to be malicious: "<hi type="italic">What accusation bring you against this man?</hi>" What is the crime you charge him with, and what proof have you of it? It was a law of nature, before Valerius Publicola made it a Roman law, <hi type="italic">Ne quis indicta causa condemnetur—No man should be condemned unheard.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Acts.25.16-Acts.25.17">Acts xxv. 16, 17</reference>. It is unreasonable to commit a man, without alleging some cause in the warrant, and much more to arraign a man when there is no bill of indictment found against him. <div eID="gen28512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28513" type="x-p"/> 2. The prosecutors demand judgment against him upon a general surmise that he was a criminal, not alleging, much less proving, any thing in particular <hi type="italic">worthy of death or of bonds</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.18.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">If he were not a malefactor,</hi> or evildoer, <hi type="italic">we would not have delivered him to thee</hi> to be condemned. This bespeaks them, (1.) Very rude and uncivil to Pilate, a company of ill-natured men, that affected to despise dominion. When Pilate was so complaisant to them as to come out to treat with them, yet they were to the highest degree out of humour with him. He put the most reasonable question to them that could be; but, if it had been the most absurd, they could not have answered him with more disdain. (2.) Very spiteful and malicious towards our Lord Jesus: right or wrong, they will have him to be a malefactor, and treated as one. We are to presume a man innocent till he is proved guilty, but they will presume him guilty who could prove himself innocent. They cannot say, "He is a traitor, a murderer, a felon, a breaker of the peace," but they say, "He is an evil-doer." He an evil-doer who <hi type="italic">went about doing good!</hi> Let those be called whom he had cured, and fed, and taught; whom he has rescued from devils, and raised from death; and let them be asked whether he be an evil-doer or no. Note, It is no new thing for the best of benefactors to be branded and run down as the worst of malefactors. (3.) Very proud and conceited of themselves, and their own judgment and justice, as if their delivering a man up, under the general character of a malefactor, were sufficient for the civil magistrate to ground a judicial sentence upon, than which what could be more haughty? <div eID="gen28513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28514" type="x-p"/> 3. The judge remands him to their own court (<reference osisRef="John.18.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Take you him, and judge him according to your</hi> own <hi type="italic">law,</hi> and do not trouble me with him." Now, (1.) Some think Pilate herein complimented them, acknowledging the remains of their power, and allowing them to exert it. Corporal punishment they might inflict, as <hi type="italic">scourging in their synagogues;</hi> whether capital or no is uncertain. "But," saith Pilate, "go as far as your law will allow you, and, if you go further, it shall be connived at." This he said, willing to do the Jews a pleasure, but unwilling to do them the service they required. (2.) Others think he bantered them, and upbraided them with their present state of weakness and subjection. They would be the sole judges of the guilt. "Pray," saith Pilate, "if you will be so, go on as you have begun; you have found him guilty by your own law, condemn him, if you dare, by your own law, to carry on the humour." Nothing is more absurd, nor more deserves to be exposed, than for those to pretend to dictate, and boast of their wisdom, who are weak and in subordinate stations, and whose lot it is to be dictated to. Some think Pilate here reflects upon the law of Moses, as if it allowed them what the Roman law would by no means allow—the judging of a man unheard. "It may be your law will suffer such a thing, but ours will not." Thus, through their corruptions, the law of God was blasphemed; and so is his gospel too. <div eID="gen28514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28515" type="x-p"/> 4. They disown any authority as judges, and (since it must be so) are content to be prosecutors. They now grow less insolent and more submissive, and own, "<hi type="italic">It is not lawful for us to put any man to death,</hi> whatever less punishment we may inflict, and this is a malefactor whom we would have the blood of." <div eID="gen28515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28516" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some think they had lost their power to give judgment in matters of life and death only by their own carelessness, and cowardly yielding to the darling iniquities of the age; so Dr. Lightfoot <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk exesti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">It is not</hi> in our power to pass sentence of death upon <hi type="italic">any,</hi> if we do, we shall have the mob about us immediately. <div eID="gen28516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28517" type="x-p"/> (2.) Others think their power was taken from them by the Romans, because they had not used it well, or because it was thought too great a trust to be lodged in the hands of a conquered and yet an unsubdued people. Their acknowledgement of this they designed for a compliment to Pilate, and to atone for their rudeness (<reference osisRef="John.18.30">v. 30</reference>), but it amounts to a full evidence that <hi type="italic">the sceptre was departed from Judah,</hi> and therefore that now the Messiah was come, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>. If the Jews have no power <hi type="italic">to put any man to death,</hi> where is the sceptre? Yet they ask not, <hi type="italic">Where is the Shiloh?</hi> <div eID="gen28517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28518" type="x-p"/> (3.) However, there was a providence in it, that either they should have not power to put any man to death, or should decline the exercise of it upon this occasion, <hi type="italic">That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying what death he should die,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.32">v. 32</reference>. Observe, [1.] In general, that even those who designed the defeating of Christ's sayings were, beyond their intention, made serviceable to the fulfilling of them by an overruling hand of God. <hi type="italic">No word of Christ shall fall to the ground;</hi> he can never either deceive or be deceived. Even <hi type="italic">the chief priests,</hi> while they persecuted him as <hi type="italic">a deceiver,</hi> had their spirit so directed as to help to prove him true, when we should think that by taking other measures they might have defeated his predictions. <hi type="italic">Howbeit, they meant not so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. [2.] Those sayings of Christ in particular were fulfilled which he had spoken concerning his own death. Two sayings of Christ concerning his death were fulfilled, by the Jews declining to <hi type="italic">judge him according to their law. First,</hi> He had said that he should be <hi type="italic">delivered to the Gentiles,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">they should put him to death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.19">Matt. xx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.33">Mark x. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.32-Luke.18.33">Luke xviii. 32, 33</reference>), and hereby that saying was fulfilled. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He had said that he should be crucified (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.19">Matt. xx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.2">xxvi. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">lifted up,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">xii. 32</reference>. Now, if they had <hi type="italic">judged him by their law,</hi> he had been stoned; burning, strangling, and beheading, were in some cases used among the Jews, but never crucifying. It was therefore necessary that Christ should be put to death by the Romans, that, being <hi type="italic">hanged upon a tree,</hi> he might be <hi type="italic">made a curse for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Gal. iii. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">his hands and feet</hi> might be <hi type="italic">pierced.</hi> As the Roman power had brought him to be born at Bethlehem, so now to die upon a cross, and both according to the scriptures. It is likewise determined concerning us, though not discovered to us, <hi type="italic">what death we shall die,</hi> which should free us from all disquieting cares about that matter. "Lord, what, and when, and how thou hast appointed." <div eID="gen28518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28519" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Pilate's conference with the prisoner, <reference osisRef="John.18.33">v. 33</reference>, &c., where we have, <div eID="gen28519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28520" type="x-p"/> 1. The prisoner set to the bar. Pilate, after he had conferred with the chief priests at his door, entered into the hall, and called for Jesus to be brought in. He would not examine him in the crowd, where he might be disturbed by the noise, but ordered him to be brought <hi type="italic">into the hall;</hi> for he made no difficulty of going in among the Gentiles. We by sin were become liable to the judgment of God, and were to be brought before his bar; therefore <hi type="italic">Christ, being made sin and a curse for us,</hi> was arraigned as a criminal. Pilate entered into judgment with him, that God might not enter into judgment with us. <div eID="gen28520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28521" type="x-p"/> 2. His examination. The other evangelists tell us that his accusers had laid it to his charge that <hi type="italic">he perverted the nation, forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar,</hi> and upon this he is examined. <div eID="gen28521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28522" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a question put to him, with a design to ensnare him and to find out something upon which to ground an accusation: "<hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews?</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho basileus</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">that king of the Jews</hi> who has been so much talked of and so long expected—Messiah the prince, art thou he? Dost thou pretend to be he? Dost thou call thyself, and wouldest thou be thought so?" For he was far from imagining that really he was so, or making a question of that. Some think Pilate asked this with an air of scorn and contempt: "What! <hi type="italic">art thou a king,</hi> who makest so mean a figure? <hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews,</hi> by whom thou art thus hated and persecuted? <hi type="italic">Art thou king de jure—of right,</hi> while the emperor is only king <hi type="italic">de facto—in fact?</hi>" Since it could not be proved he ever said it, he would constrain him to say it now, that he might proceed upon his own confession. <div eID="gen28522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28523" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ answers this question with another; not for evasion, but as an intimation to Pilate to consider what he did, and upon what grounds he went (<reference osisRef="John.18.34">v. 34</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Sayest thou this thing of thyself,</hi> from a suspicion arising in thy own breast, <hi type="italic">or did others tell it thee of me,</hi> and dost thou ask it only to oblige them?" [1.] "It is plain that thou hast no reason to <hi type="italic">say this of thyself.</hi>" Pilate was bound by his office to take care of the interests of the Roman government, but he could not say that this was in any danger, or suffered any damage, from any thing our Lord Jesus had ever said or done. He never appeared in worldly pomp, never assumed any secular power, never acted as a judge or divider; never were any traitorous principles or practices objected to him, nor any thing that might give the least shadow of suspicion. [2.] "If others <hi type="italic">tell it thee of me,</hi> to incense thee against me, thou oughtest to consider who they are, and upon what principles they go, and whether those who represent me as an <hi type="italic">enemy to Cæsar</hi> are not really such themselves, and therefore use this only as a pretence to cover their malice, for, if so, the matter ought to be well weighed by a judge that would do justice." Nay, if Pilate had been as inquisitive as he ought to have been in this matter, he would have found that the true reason why the chief priests were outrageous against Jesus was because he did not set up a temporal kingdom in opposition to the Roman power; if he would have done this, and would have wrought miracles to bring the Jews out of the Roman bondage, as Moses did to bring them out of the Egyptian, they would have been so far from siding with the Romans against him that they would have made him their king, and have fought under him against the Romans; but, not answering this expectation of theirs, they charged that upon him of which they were themselves most notoriously guilty-disaffection to and design against the present government; and was such an information as this fit to be countenanced? <div eID="gen28523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28524" type="x-p"/> (3.) Pilate resents Christ's answer, and takes it very ill, <reference osisRef="John.18.35">v. 35</reference>. This is a direct answer to Christ's question, <reference osisRef="John.18.34">v. 34</reference>. [1.] Christ had asked him whether he spoke of himself. "No," says he; "<hi type="italic">am I a Jew,</hi> that thou suspectest me to be in the plot against thee? I know nothing of the Messiah, nor desire to know, and therefore interest not myself in the dispute who is the Messiah and who not; the dispute who is the Messiah and who not; it is all alike to me." Observe with what disdain Pilate asks, <hi type="italic">Am I a Jew?</hi> The Jews were, upon many accounts, an honourable people; but, having corrupted the covenant of their God, <hi type="italic">he made them contemptible and base before all the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.8-Mal.2.9">Mal. ii. 8, 9</reference>), so that a man of sense and honour reckoned it a scandal to be counted a Jew. Thus good names often suffer for the sake of the bad men that wear them. It is sad that when a Turk is suspected of dishonesty he should ask, "What! do you take me for a Christian?" [2.] Christ had asked him whether others told him. "Yes," says he, "and those <hi type="italic">thine own people,</hi> who, one would think would be biased in favour of thee, and <hi type="italic">the priests,</hi> whose testimony, <hi type="italic">in verbum sacerdotis—on the word of a priest,</hi> ought to be regarded; and therefore I have nothing to do but to proceed upon their information." Thus Christ, in his religion, still suffers by those that are of his own nation, even the priests, that profess relation to him, but do not live up to their profession. [3.] Christ had declined answering that question, <hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews?</hi> And therefore Pilate puts another question to him more general, "<hi type="italic">What hast thou done?</hi> What provocation hast thou given to thy own nation, and particularly the priests, to be so violent against thee? Surely there cannot be all this smoke without some fire, what is it?" <div eID="gen28524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28525" type="x-p"/> (4.) Christ, in his next reply, gives a more full and direct answer to Pilate's former question, <hi type="italic">Art thou a king?</hi> explaining in what sense he was a king, but not such a king as was any ways dangerous to the Roman government, not a secular king, for his interest was not supported by secular methods, <reference osisRef="John.18.36">v. 36</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen28525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28526" type="x-p"/> [1.] An account of the nature and constitution of Christ's kingdom: It <hi type="italic">is not of this world.</hi> It is expressed negatively to rectify the present mistakes concerning it; but the positive is implied, it is <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven,</hi> and belongs to another world. Christ is a king, and has a kingdom, but <hi type="italic">not of this world. First</hi> Its rise is not from this world; the kingdoms of men arise <hi type="italic">out of the sea and the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.3">Dan. vii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1 Rev.13.11">Rev. xiii. 1, 11</reference>); but <hi type="italic">the holy city comes from God out of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev. xxii. 2</reference>. His kingdom is not by succession, election, or conquest, but by the immediate and special designation of the divine will and counsel. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Its nature is not worldly; it is a kingdom within men (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.21">Luke xvi. 21</reference>), set up in their hearts and consciences (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Rom. xiv. 17</reference>), its riches spiritual, its powers spiritual, and <hi type="italic">all its glory within.</hi> The ministers of state in Christ's kingdom have not <hi type="italic">the spirit of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1 Cor. ii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Its guards and supports are not worldly; its weapons are spiritual. It neither needed nor used secular force to maintain and advance it, nor was it carried on in a way <hi type="italic">hurtful to kings or provinces;</hi> it did not in the least interfere with the prerogatives of princes nor the property of their subjects; it tended not to alter any national establishment in secular things, nor opposed any kingdom but that of sin and Satan. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Its tendency and design are not worldly. Christ neither aimed nor would allow his disciples to aim at the pomp and power of <hi type="italic">the great men of the earth. Fifthly,</hi> Its subjects, though they are in the world, yet <hi type="italic">are not of the world;</hi> they <hi type="italic">are called and chosen out of the world,</hi> are born from, and bound for, another world; they are neither the world's pupils nor its darlings, neither governed by its wisdom nor enriched with its wealth. <div eID="gen28526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28527" type="x-p"/> [2.] An evidence of the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom produced. If he had designed an opposition to the government, he would have fought them at their own weapons, and would have repelled force with force of the same nature; but he did not take this course: <hi type="italic">If my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews,</hi> and my kingdom be ruined by them. But, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His followers did not offer to fight; there was no uproar, no attempt to rescue him, though the town was now full of Galileans, his friends and countrymen, and they were generally armed; but the peaceable behaviour of his disciples on this occasion was enough <hi type="italic">to put to silence the ignorance of foolish men. Secondly,</hi> He did not order them to fight; nay, he forbade them, which was an evidence both that he did not depend upon worldly aids (for he could have summoned <hi type="italic">legions of angels</hi> into his service, which showed that his <hi type="italic">kingdom was from above</hi>), and also that he did not dread worldly opposition, for he was very willing to be <hi type="italic">delivered to the Jews,</hi> as knowing that what would have been the destruction of any worldly kingdom would be the advancement and establishment of his; justly therefore does he conclude, <hi type="italic">Now</hi> you may see <hi type="italic">my kingdom is not from hence;</hi> in the world but not of it. <div eID="gen28527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28528" type="x-p"/> (5.) In answer to Pilate's further query, he replies yet more directly, <reference osisRef="John.18.37">v. 37</reference>, where we have, [1.] Pilate's plain question: "<hi type="italic">Art thou a king then?</hi> Thou speakest of a kingdom thou hast; art thou then, in any sense, a king? And what colour hast thou for such a claim? Explain thyself." [2.] The good confession which our Lord Jesus witnessed before Pontius Pilate, in answer to this (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">1 Tim. vi. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou sayest that I am a king,</hi> that is, It is as thou sayest, I am a king; for <hi type="italic">I came to bear witness of the truth. First,</hi> He grants himself to be a king, though not in the sense that Pilate meant. The Messiah was expected under the character of a king, <hi type="italic">Messiah the prince;</hi> and therefore, having owned to Caiaphas that he was the Christ, he would not disown to Pilate that he was king, lest he should seem inconsistent with himself. Note, Though Christ <hi type="italic">took upon him the form of a servant,</hi> yet even then he justly claimed the honour and authority of a king. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He explains himself, and shows how he is a king, as <hi type="italic">he came to bear witness of the truth;</hi> he rules in the minds of men by the power of truth. If he had meant to declare himself a temporal prince, he would have said, <hi type="italic">For this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world,</hi> to rule the nations, to conquer kings, and to take possession of kingdoms; no, <hi type="italic">he came to be a witness,</hi> a witness for the God that made the world, and against sin that ruins the world, and by this <hi type="italic">word of his testimony</hi> he sets up, and keeps up, his kingdom. It was foretold that he should be <hi type="italic">a witness to the people,</hi> and, as such, <hi type="italic">a leader and commander to the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa. lv. 4</reference>. Christ's kingdom was not of this world, in which <hi type="italic">truth faileth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.15">Isa. lix. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare—He that cannot dissemble knows not how to reign</hi>), but of that world in which truth reigns eternally. Christ's errand into the world, and his business in the world, were <hi type="italic">to bear witness to the truth.</hi> 1. To reveal it, to discover to the world that which otherwise could not have been known concerning God and his will and <hi type="italic">good-will to men,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.26">xvii. 26</reference>. 2. To confirm it, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.8">Rom. xv. 8</reference>. By his miracles <hi type="italic">he bore witness to the truth</hi> of religion, the truth of divine revelation, and of God's perfections and providence, and the truth of his promise and covenant, <hi type="italic">that all men through him might believe.</hi> Now by doing this he is a king, and sets up a kingdom. (1.) The foundation and power, the spirit and genius, of Christ's kingdom, is truth, divine truth. When he said, <hi type="italic">I am the truth,</hi> he said, in effect, I am a king. He conquers by the convincing evidence of truth; he rules by the commanding power of truth, and <hi type="italic">in his majesty rides prosperously, because of truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">Ps. xlv. 4</reference>. It is with his truth that he shall judge the people, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">Ps. xcvi. 13</reference>. It is the sceptre of his kingdom; he <hi type="italic">draws with the cords of a man,</hi> with truth revealed to us, and received by us in <hi type="italic">the love of it;</hi> and thus he <hi type="italic">brings thoughts into obedience.</hi> He came <hi type="italic">a light into the world,</hi> and rules as the sun by day. (2.) The subjects of this kingdom are those that are <hi type="italic">of the truth.</hi> All that by the grace of God are rescued from under the power of <hi type="italic">the father of lies,</hi> and are disposed to receive the truth and submit to the power and influence of it, will hear Christ's voice, will become his subjects, and will bear faith and true allegiance to him. Every one that has any real sense of true religion will entertain the Christian religion, and they belong to his kingdom; by the power of truth he makes them willing, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">Ps. xc. 3</reference>. All that are in love with truth will hear the voice of Christ, for greater, better, surer, sweeter truths can nowhere be found than are found in Christ, by whom <hi type="italic">grace and truth came;</hi> so that, by <hi type="italic">hearing Christ's voice,</hi> we know that we are <hi type="italic">of the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.19">1 John iii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen28528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28529" type="x-p"/> (6.) Pilate, hereupon, puts a good question to him, but does not stay for an answer, <reference osisRef="John.18.38">v. 38</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">What is truth?</hi> and <hi type="italic">immediately went out again.</hi> <div eID="gen28529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28530" type="x-p"/> [1.] It is certain that this was a good question, and could not be put to one that was better able to answer it. Truth is that <hi type="italic">pearl of great price</hi> which the human understanding has a desire for and is in quest of; for it cannot rest but in that which is, or at least is apprehended to be, truth. When we <hi type="italic">search the scriptures,</hi> and attend the ministry of the word, it must be with this enquiry, <hi type="italic">What is truth?</hi> and with this prayer, <hi type="italic">Lead me in thy truth, into all truth.</hi> But many put this question that have not patience and constancy enough to persevere in their search after truth, or not humility and sincerity enough to receive it when they have found it, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.7">2 Tim. iii. 7</reference>. Thus many deal with their own consciences; they ask them those needful questions, "What am I?" "What have I done?" but will not take time for an answer. <div eID="gen28530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28531" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is uncertain with what design Pilate asked this question. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Perhaps he spoke it as a learner, as one that began to think well of Christ, and to look upon him with some respect, and desired to be informed what new notions he advanced and what improvements he pretended to in religion and learning. But while he desired to hear some new truth from him, as Herod to see some miracle, the clamour and outrage of the priests' mob at his gate obliged him abruptly to let fall the discourse. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Some think he spoke it as a judge, enquiring further into the cause now brought before him: "Let me into this mystery, and tell me what the truth of it is, the true state of this matter." <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Others think he spoke it as a scoffer, in a jeering way: "Thou talkest of truth; canst thou tell what truth is, or give me a definition of it?" Thus he makes a jest of the everlasting gospel, that great truth which the chief priests hated and persecuted, and which Christ was now witnessing to and suffering for; and like men of no religion, who take a pleasure in bantering all religions, he ridicules both sides; and therefore Christ made him no reply. <hi type="italic">Answer not a fool according to his folly; cast not pearls before swine.</hi> But, though Christ would not tell Pilate what is truth, he has told his disciples, and by them has told us, <reference osisRef="John.14.6">ch. xiv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen28531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28532" type="x-p"/> III. The result of both these conferences with the prosecutors and the prisoner (<reference osisRef="John.18.38-John.18.40">v. 38-40</reference>), in two things:— <div eID="gen28532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28533" type="x-p"/> 1. The judge appeared his friend, and favourable to him, for, <div eID="gen28533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28534" type="x-p"/> (1.) He publicly declared him innocent, <reference osisRef="John.18.38">v. 38</reference>. Upon the whole matter, <hi type="italic">I find in him no fault at all.</hi> He supposes there might be some controversy in religion between him and them, wherein he was as likely to be in the right as they; but nothing criminal appears against him. This solemn declaration of Christ's innocency was, [1.] For the justification and honour of the Lord Jesus. By this it appears that though he was treated as the worst of malefactors he had never merited such treatment. [2.] For explaining the design and intention of his death, that he did not die for any sin of his own, even in the judgement of the judge himself, and therefore he died as a sacrifice for our sins, and that, even in the judgment of the prosecutors themselves, <hi type="italic">one man should die for the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.50">ch. xi. 50</reference>. This is he that <hi type="italic">did no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa. liii. 9</reference>), who was to <hi type="italic">be cut off, but not for himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>. [3.] For aggravating the sin of the Jews that prosecuted him with so much violence. If a prisoner has had a fair trial, and has been acquitted by those that are proper judges of the crime, especially if there be no cause to suspect them partial in his favour, he must be believed innocent, and his accusers are bound to acquiesce. But our Lord Jesus, though brought in not guilty, is still run down as a malefactor, and his blood thirsted for. <div eID="gen28534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28535" type="x-p"/> (2.) He proposed an expedient for his discharge (<reference osisRef="John.18.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have a custom, that I should release to you a prisoner at the passover;</hi> shall it be this king of the Jews? He proposed this, not to the chief priests (he knew they would never agree to it), but to the multitude; it was an appeal to the people, as appears, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.15">Matt. xxvii. 15</reference>. Probably he had heard how this Jesus had been attended but the other day with the hosannas of the common people; he therefore looked upon him to be the darling of the multitude, and the envy only of the rulers, and therefore he made no doubt but they would demand the release of Jesus, and this would stop the mouth of the prosecutors, and all would be well. [1.] He allows their custom, for which, perhaps, they had had a long prescription, in honour of the passover, which was a memorial of their release. But it was adding to God's words, as if he had not instituted enough for the due commemoration of that deliverance, and, though an act of mercy, might be injustice to the public, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.15">Prov. xvii. 15</reference>. [2.] He offers to release Jesus to them, according to the custom. If Pilate had had the honesty and courage that became a judge, he would not have named an innocent person to be competitor with a notorious criminal for this favour; if he <hi type="italic">found no fault in him,</hi> he was bound in conscience to discharge him. But he was willing to trim the matter, and please all sides, being governed more by worldly wisdom than by the rules of equity. <div eID="gen28535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28536" type="x-p"/> 2. The people appeared his enemies, and implacable against him (<reference osisRef="John.18.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">They cried all again</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Not this man,</hi> let not him be released, <hi type="italic">but Barabbas.</hi> Observe, (1.) How fierce and outrageous they were. Pilate proposed the thing to them calmly, as worthy their mature consideration, but they resolved it in a heat, and gave in their resolution with clamour and noise, and in the utmost confusion. Note, The enemies of Christ's holy religion cry it down, and so hope to run it down; witness the outcry at Ephesus, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.34">Acts xix. 34</reference>. But those who think the worse of things or persons merely for their being thus exclaimed against have a very small share of constancy and consideration. Nay, there is cause to suspect a deficiency of reason and justice on that side which calls in the assistance of popular tumult. (2.) How foolish and absurd they were, as is intimated in the short account here given of the other candidate: <hi type="italic">Now Barabbas was a robber,</hi> and therefore, [1.] A breaker of the law of God; and yet he shall be spared, rather than one who reproved the pride, avarice, and tyranny of the priests and elders. Though Barabbas be a robber, he will not rob them of Moses's seat, nor of their traditions, and then no matter. [2.] He was an enemy to the public safety and personal property. The clamour of the town is wont to be against robbers (<reference osisRef="Job.30.5">Job xxx. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Men cried after them as after a thief</hi>), yet here it is for one. Thus those do who prefer their sins before Christ. Sin is a robber, every base lust is a robber, and yet foolishly chosen rather than Christ, who would truly enrich us.  <chapter eID="John.18"/> <div eID="gen28536" type="x-p"/>

Betrayal and Apprehension of Jesus.</title> <div sID="gen29649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15405"/><hi type="bold">1-3. over the brook Kedron--</hi>a deep, dark ravine, to the northeast of Jerusalem, through which flowed this small storm brook or winter torrent, and which in summer is dried up.<div eID="gen29649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">where was a garden--</hi>at the foot of the Mount of Olives, "called Gethsemane; that is, olive press (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.30">Mt 26:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.36">36</reference>). <div eID="gen29650" type="x-p"/>
entries.a28b179aa19f07237b3f5a74f240b32542655c22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15408"/><div sID="gen29657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15408"/><hi type="bold">4-9. Jesus ... knowing all things that should come--</hi>were coming.<div eID="gen29657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon him, went forth--</hi>from the shade of the trees, probably, into open view, indicating His sublime preparedness to meet His captors.<div eID="gen29658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Whom seek ye?--</hi>partly to prevent a rush of the soldiery upon the disciples [Bengel]; and see <reference osisRef="Mark.14.51">Mr 14:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.52">52</reference>, as showing a tendency to this: but still more as part of that courage and majesty which so overawed them. He would not wait to be taken. <div eID="gen29659" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa9cfbfa8fa0faa476927e99c5749f893a7ed4b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15414"/><div sID="gen29669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15414"/><hi type="bold">10-11. Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it, and smote the high priest's servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant's name was Malchus--</hi>None of the other Evangelists mention the name either of the ardent disciple or of his victim. John being "known to the high priest" (<reference osisRef="John.18.15">Joh 18:15</reference>), the mention of the servant's name by him is quite natural, and an interesting mark of truth in a small matter. As to the right ear, specified both here and in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.50">Lu 22:50</reference>), the man was "likely foremost of those who advanced to seize Jesus, and presented himself in the attitude of a combatant; hence his right side would be exposed to attack. The blow of Peter was evidently aimed vertically at his head" [Webster and Wilkinson]. <div eID="gen29669" type="x-p"/>
entries.87f6e05fd368232139f29fcbc479e1883fef2d7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15416"/><div sID="gen29672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15416"/><hi type="bold">12. entries.fb50bd1fb48617ef8f9cd3155774eafc73707cd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15417"/><div sID="gen29673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15417"/><hi type="bold">13. And led him away--</hi>"In that hour," says Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.55">Mt 26:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">56</reference>), and probably now, on the way to judgment, when the crowds were pressing upon Him, "said Jesus to the multitudes, Are ye come out as against a thief, with swords and staves, for to take Me"--expressive of the indignity which He felt to be thus done to Him--"I sat daily with you in the temple, and ye laid no hold on Me. But this" (adds <reference osisRef="Luke.22.53">Lu 22:53</reference>) "is your hour and the power of darkness." Matthew continues--"But all this was done that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples forsook Him and fled" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">Mt 26:56</reference>)--thus fulfilling His prediction (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.27">Mr 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.32">Joh 16:32</reference>). <div eID="gen29673" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15418"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.18.13-John.18.27">Joh 18:13-27</reference>. Jesus before Annas and Caiaphas--Fall of Peter.</title> <div sID="gen29674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15418"/><hi type="bold">13-14. And led him away to Annas first--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.3.2">Lu 3:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Matt.26.57">Mt 26:57</reference>). (Also see on <reference osisRef="Mark.14.53">Mr 14:53</reference>.) <div eID="gen29674" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfc941a64d7ceba631cea128f8fa52e94521f6b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15420"/><div sID="gen29676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15420"/><hi type="bold">15-18. Simon Peter followed Jesus--</hi>Natural though this was, and safe enough, had he only "watched and prayed that he enter not into temptation," as his Master bade him (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.41">Mt 26:41</reference>), it was, in his case, a fatal step.<div eID="gen29676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ... another disciple--</hi>Rather, "the other disciple"--our Evangelist himself, no doubt.<div eID="gen29677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known unto the high priest--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.18.10">Joh 18:10</reference>).<div eID="gen29678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29679" type="x-p"/> went in with Jesus into the palace of the high priest. <div eID="gen29679" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6cbb3b48872bd9d5c6b084361c8c36ccf2d2fe7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15424"/><div sID="gen29688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15424"/><hi type="bold">19-21. From our Lord's answer it would seem that "His disciples" were understood to be some secret party. (Also see on <reference osisRef="Mark.14.54">Mr 14:54</reference>.) <div eID="gen29688" type="x-p"/>
