               <ns0:p n="19">19 ¶ The high priest then asked Jesus of his disciples, and of his doctrine <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Questions about <ns0:hi>Sedition</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Rebellion,</ns0:hi> belonged not to the <ns0:hi>Iudge</ns0:hi> of this Court, but <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ell under the Cognisance of the <ns0:hi>Roman Governor,</ns0:hi> they being now a Conquered people, and Tributary to the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi>; who, tho themselves <ns0:hi>Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thens,</ns0:hi> granted the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> their liberty as to Religion, and Courts in order thereunto; as also a liberty of Courts for civil causes: the <ns0:hi>High Priest</ns0:hi> therefore saith nothing to Christ about his <ns0:hi>being a King,</ns0:hi> but onely inquireth of him about his <ns0:hi>Doctrine</ns0:hi>; what particular questions he propounded to him, we do not read; onely in general he inquired about the Doctrine he had Preached, and the <ns0:hi>Disciples</ns0:hi> he had sent out, which was one and the same cause, to see if he could bring him under the guilt of a <ns0:hi>false Prophet</ns0:hi>; for that, and <ns0:hi>Blaspemy,</ns0:hi> and Idolatry, were three principal causes that fell under the Cognisance of this Court, as appeareth from <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Jesus answered him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7.26</ns0:note>, I spake openly to the world <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To all sorts of men, my Enemies as well as my Friends.</ns0:note>; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sort <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> for instruction do use to resort to the <ns0:hi>Temple,</ns0:hi> which was in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and whither three times in the year, all the Males were wont to come from all parts of the Countrey; and in the publick assemblies of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and in the places where they use to meet:</ns0:note>, and in secret have I said nothing <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">I have said no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing in secret, contrary to the Doctrine which I have pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lickly taught; tho I have Preached in other places, yet it hath been the same thing which I have said in pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lick.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Why askest thou me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">We are told by those that have written about the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> order in their Courts of Judgment; <ns0:hi>That their Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pital causes always began with the defensative part; and that it was lawful for any to speak for the defendants, for a whole day together</ns0:hi>; (tho they did not observe this in the cause of Christ) and their method was not to put the <ns0:hi>Defendents</ns0:hi> to accuse themselves, but to examine witnesses against them; Our Saviour therefore appeals to their own order, and says, <ns0:hi>Why askest thou me?</ns0:hi> It was, saith he, no secret action; I spake publickly, ask them that heard me speak, they know what Doctrine I preached, and can accuse me if I delivered any false Doctrine.</ns0:note>? ask them which heard me, what I have said unto them: behold, they know what I said <ns0:hi>b</ns0:hi>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And when he had thus spoken, one of the of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficers which stood by <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 20.2. Acts 23.2.</ns0:note>, stroke Jesus <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, With a rod.</ns0:note> with the palm of his hand, saying, Answerest thou the high priest so <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This lets us see in what indecent disorder the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Government was at this time, that an inferior Officer dared to strike a supposed Criminal, standing before the Judgment-seat, and defending himself from their own known rules and methods; for what had our Saviour said or done, more than making use of the liberty their own Law allowed, not confessing any thing against himself, but putting them upon the proof of what they laid to his charge? yet we read no notice taken of this disorder.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Our Saviour could easily have revenged himself upon this Officer; but to teach us our duty, he onely gently re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proves him; and lets him know, that he did not behave himself as one ought to do in the face of a Court of Justice, where he had both a liberty, and a present opportunity to have accused him, if he had spoken ill; and if he had spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken well, there was no reason for his striking him.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 (<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 26.57.</ns0:note> Now Annas had sent him bound unto Cai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />aphas the high priest <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The words in the 24<ns0:hi>th. ver.</ns0:hi> are onely to let us know, that these things were not done before <ns0:hi>Annas,</ns0:hi> but before <ns0:hi>Caiaphas</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>High Priest,</ns0:hi> to whom (as to his proper Judg) <ns0:hi>Annas</ns0:hi> had sent him bound, as he was at first brought to him.</ns0:note>).</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And Simon Peter stood and warmed him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self: They said therefore unto him, Art not thou also one of his disciples? He denied it, and said, I am not.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 One of the servants of the high priest be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:368" />
his kinsman, whose ear Peter cut off saith, Did I not see thee in the garden with him?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Peter then denied again, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13.38.</ns0:note> immediately the cock crew <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This History of <ns0:hi>Peters</ns0:hi> denial of his Master the second time, we have before met with, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.69, 70, 71. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14.69, 70. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.58, 59. with several circumstances not mentioned by <ns0:hi>Iohn.</ns0:hi> See the notes upon <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> 26.69, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 ¶ <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.2.</ns0:note> Then led they Jesus from Caiaphas unto <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, Pilates House.</ns0:note> the hall of judgment <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Chief Priests having in their <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim</ns0:hi> done with our Saviours case, and judg'd him <ns0:hi>worthy of death,</ns0:hi> as we read <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.66. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14.64. which two Evangelists, with <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> relate this History of Christs Tryal before the <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim,</ns0:hi> with many more circumstances than <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> doth, (see the notes on those Texts) they now lead him from the <ns0:hi>Ecclesiastical</ns0:hi> Court, to the Court of the Civil Magistrate; either kept in <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> House, who was the present civil Governor under the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> or some where at least where he sat as Judge; which was therefore called the <ns0:hi>Hall of Iudgment.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and it was early <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">How early it was, we cannot tell, but early i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> was; probably about five or six of the Clock.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Acts 10.28. and 11 3.</ns0:note>, and they themselves went not into the judgment-hall, lest they should be defiled: but that they might eat the passover <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> would not go into the Judgment-hall, that they might not be defiled, for they accounted a <ns0:hi>legal pollution</ns0:hi> and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cleanness to come into an <ns0:hi>Heathens</ns0:hi> House, or to touch any thing which an <ns0:hi>Heathen</ns0:hi> had touched; now the reason is assigned why they were afraid of contracting any legal pol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lution, <ns0:hi>viz. That they might eat the Passover.</ns0:hi> Obj. <ns0:hi>But had they not eaten the Passover the night before; that was the time prescribed by the Law, to the latter of which there is no doubt but that our Saviour strictly kept himself? Ans.</ns0:hi> Some say, that they had not, because, the day wherein they should have eaten it, this year, falling the day before their Sabbath, the Passover was put off to be kept on the Sabbath, that two great Festivals might not be kept two days succes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sively; so as, tho our Saviour kept it at the time appointed by the Law, yet the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> did not. But this is denied by o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />other very Learned men, who tell us, the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> never alte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red their day for keeping their Passover, neither for the suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding Sabbath, nor any other reason. They say there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore, that by the <ns0:hi>Passover</ns0:hi> which is mentioned in this Verse, is to be understood, <ns0:hi>The Feast</ns0:hi> mentioned, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 28.17. which was to be kept the <ns0:hi>fifteenth day,</ns0:hi> which day was a day of great solemnity with them from the morning to the evening; all the seven days they also offered various Sacri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fices, which all went under the name of the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they followed in the days of the Paschal Feast. Thus the term <ns0:hi>Passover</ns0:hi> is taken, Deut. 16.2. <ns0:hi>Thou shalt there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore sacrifice the Passover unto the Lord thy God, of the flock and the herd.</ns0:hi> According to this Notion, the meaning of those words, <ns0:hi>that they might eat the Passover,</ns0:hi> is, That they might proceed in their <ns0:hi>Paschal solemnity,</ns0:hi> keeping the Feast according to the Law. Be it as it will, these Hypo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crites in it notoriously discovered their hypocrisie, scrupling what caused a legal uncleanness, and not at all scrupling either immediately before their eating the Passover, or pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sently after it, in their great Festival to defile themselves with the guilt of Innocent blood; nay, had Christ been such a malefactor as they pretended, yet the bringing him into judgment, their prosecuting, and accusing, and condemning him, and assisting in his Crucifying, were not works fit for the day before such a Solemnity, or the day after it, which was so great a Festival; but there is nothing more or<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>inary, than for persons over <ns0:hi>zealous</ns0:hi> as to <ns0:hi>Rituals,</ns0:hi> to be as remiss with reference to <ns0:hi>Moral duties.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Pilate then went out unto them, and said, What accusation bring you against this man <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Governor humoureth them in their super<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stition; (the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> having granted them the liberty of their Religion) they scruple to go in to the ordinary place of judgment; he goes out to them, and calls for their <ns0:hi>Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cusation</ns0:hi> of Christ, according to the ordinary and regular course of judgments.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 They answered and said unto him, If he were not a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                     <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>lefactor, we would not have deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered him up unto thee <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">They had in their <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim</ns0:hi> before, judged him guilty of <ns0:hi>Blasphemy, Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.65. but this they durst not men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, lest <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> should have rejected them, as being not concerned in questions of their Law; they therefore onely exclaim against him in the general as a great Malefactor; but of what kind, they do not say. It should seem they would have had <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> have added his civil Authority, to confirm and execute their Ecclesiastical censure, without so much as hearing any thing of the cause, (altho at this day frequent in <ns0:hi>Popish</ns0:hi> Countries) but they met with a more equal Judge.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">I will judge no man before my self first hear, and judge of his crime; you have a Law amongst your selves, and a liberty to question and judge men upon it, proceed against him according to your Law.</ns0:note>. The Jews therefore said unto him, it is not lawful for us to put any man to death <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">They reply, It was not lawful for them to put any man to death: We are as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sured by such as are exercised in the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Writings, That <ns0:hi>the power of putting any to death, was taken away from the</ns0:hi> Jews <ns0:hi>forty years before the D<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>struction of</ns0:hi> Jerusalem. Some say, it was not taken away by the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> but by their own <ns0:hi>Court</ns0:hi>: They thought it so horrid a thing to put an <ns0:hi>Israelite</ns0:hi> to death, that wickedness of all sorts grew to such an heighth amongst them, through the impunity, or too light punishment of Criminals, that their Courts durst nor execute their just Authority. And at last their great Court determined against the putting any to death; nor (as they say) was any put to death by the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> but in some popular Tumult, after their Court had prejudiced the person by pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nouncing him guilty of <ns0:hi>Blasphemy,</ns0:hi> or some capital Crime: which seemeth the case of <ns0:hi>Stephen, Acts</ns0:hi> 7.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 33.</ns0:note> That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled which he spake, signifying what death he should die <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Christ had before this time told his Disciples that he should die, and that by the death of the Cross, as we read <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.19. God by his Providence ordereth things ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cordingly, to let us know, that the Scripture might be ful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filled to every tittle; <ns0:hi>Crucifying</ns0:hi> was no <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> but a <ns0:hi>Ro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man</ns0:hi> death; had the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> put him to death, they would have stoned him; but he must remove the curse from us, by be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing made a <ns0:hi>curse for us,</ns0:hi> being <ns0:hi>hanged on a tree,</ns0:hi> which was lookt upon as an accursed death, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.13. The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore knowing nothing of this Counsel of God, yet execute it, by refusing themselves to put him to death, and putting it off to <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> tho possibly their design was but to avoid the <ns0:hi>odium</ns0:hi> of it. Thus God maketh the wrath of men to praise him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.11.</ns0:note> Then Pilate entred into the judgment-hall again <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The ordinary place of Judicature, from whence we read before he went out, in civility to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> whose su<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perstition (as we before heard) kept them from going there during the Festival:</ns0:note>, and called Jesus, and said unto him, Art thou the king of the Jews <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He called Jesus to him privately, and asks him, if he owned himself to be the King of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi>? The confessing of which, (for without doubt they had sug<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gested some such thing to <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> and could not prove it) had brought Christ under <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> power, he being Gover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nor for the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> and so concerned to inquire upon any that pretended to any Regal Power over that Conquered people.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 Jesus answered him, Sayest thou this thing of thy self, or did others tell it thee of me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Our Saviour neither affirmeth nor denieth: tho we be bound when ever we speak, to speak the truth, yet we are not bound at all times to speak the whole truth. Our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour desireth to be satisfied from <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> whether he asked him as a private person for his own satisfaction, or as a <ns0:hi>Iudge,</ns0:hi> having received any such accusation against him? For if he asked him as a <ns0:hi>Iudge,</ns0:hi> he was bound to call them to the proof of what they had charged him with</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 Pilate answered, Am I a Jew? Thine own nation, and the chief priests have delivered thee un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to me: What hast thou done <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The sum of this is no more, than that he did not devise this captious question, for he was no <ns0:hi>Iew</ns0:hi>; nor concerned in, nor regarding what they had in their books of the Law and the Prophets; but he was accused to him by those of his own Nation: and he was desirous to find out the truth, and to know what he had done.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Tim. 6.13.</ns0:note> Jesus answered <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Chap. 6.15.</ns0:note>, My kingdom is not of this world <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That is, I cannot deny, but that I am the <ns0:hi>King of the Iews,</ns0:hi> but not in the sense they take it; not such a King as they look for in their <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi>; my Kingdom is Spiritual, o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver the hearts and minds of men, not earthly and Worldly. And of this thou thy self mayest be convinced;</ns0:note>: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">for was there ever an earthly Prince apprehended, and bound, for whom none of his Subjects would take up Arms? Here's none of my Disciples takes up Arms, or offereth to fight for me; which is a plain evidence, that I pretend to no Kingly Power in disturbance of the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Government.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:368" />37 Pilate therefore said unto him, Art thou a King then <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> seems to have spoken this, rather in derision and mockery, than out of any desire to catch him in his words:</ns0:note>? Jesus answered, Thou sayest that I am a King <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Christ neither owneth himself to be a King, nor yet denieth it, but tells <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> that he <ns0:hi>said so</ns0:hi>; and to this end he was born, <ns0:hi>and for this cause he came into the world,</ns0:hi> to bear testimony to the truth. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I cannot deny but that I have a Spiritual Kingdom, that is <ns0:hi>truth,</ns0:hi> and I must attest the truth;</ns0:note>. To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">It was a part of my errand into the World;</ns0:note>. Every one that is of the truth, heareth my voice <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">and every one who is by Divine grace disposed to believe, and love the truth, will hear and obey my Doctrine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 ¶ Pilate saith unto him, What is truth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> (as prophane persons use to do) thought that our Saviour speaking of <ns0:hi>truth,</ns0:hi> and a Spiritual Kingdom, did but <ns0:hi>Cant,</ns0:hi> and therefore asking him, what he meant by truth, he never stays for an answer, but goes out again to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> whom he had left without the door of the Judgment-hall, and</ns0:note>? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.24. Luke 23.4.</ns0:note>, I find in him no fault at all <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">tells them he found no fault in him. Whatever the quality of the Kingdom was, of which our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour spake, he judged that his pretensions to it were not prejudicial to the Authority of the Emperor, nor the Tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quility of the State; and would have dismist him from their unjust prosecution.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 15.6.</ns0:note> But ye have a custom that I should re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lease unto you one at the passover: will ye there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore that I release unto you the King of the Jews <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Whence this custom came is uncertain; most probably from the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> who in some honour of this great Festi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />val of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and in humor of them, granted them the life of any Criminal whom they desired: <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> propounds <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> as the prisoner whom he had most mind to release, perceiving that his prosecution was of malice, rather than for any just cause.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 3.14.</ns0:note> Then cried they all again, saying, Not this man but Barabbas. Now <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Luke 23.19.</ns0:note> Barabbas was a robber <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">But such was the malice of his Adversaries, that tho <ns0:hi>Barabbas</ns0:hi> was one that had committed murder in an Insur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection, yet they chuse him rather than Christ. (See the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.15, 16, 17, 18.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
